title: Cities of Kazakhstan: A Comparison
paragraphs: Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country, and within its vast territory lie cities of remarkably different characters. Almaty and Astana — now known as Astana again after briefly being called Nur-Sultan — are the two most discussed cities in the country. But for students at WKU in Uralsk, the comparison is often more personal: how does their city measure up?

Almaty is larger, louder, and more cosmopolitan than any other Kazakhstani city. It sits at the foot of the Tian Shan mountains, making it one of the most dramatically beautiful cities in Central Asia. The winters are milder than in most of Kazakhstan, and the summers are warmer and greener. Almaty has more universities, more cafés, more museums, and more international connections than Uralsk. For ambitious students, it often feels like the natural destination.

Astana, however, is arguably the most ambitious city in Kazakhstan. Built largely from scratch in the 1990s and 2000s on the flat steppe of central Kazakhstan, it is one of the youngest capital cities in the world. Its architecture is more futuristic than Almaty's — enormous glass domes, giant tents, and golden towers. In winter, it is also the coldest city in Kazakhstan, with temperatures regularly dropping below minus thirty. "Astana is more impressive than Almaty," says Amir, "but it's also less comfortable."

Uralsk — officially Oral — is smaller than both cities but has its own distinct character. It is one of the oldest cities in western Kazakhstan, with a history stretching back more than four centuries. The city sits at the edge of the European steppe, closer to Russia than to Almaty. "Uralsk is quieter," says Kamila, "and for me, quieter is better when I'm studying. There are fewer distractions."

Each city attracts different kinds of people. Almaty attracts creatives, entrepreneurs, and those who want to be at the centre of culture and business. Astana draws civil servants, diplomats, and those interested in politics and government. Uralsk, quieter and more manageable, is a place where WKU students build deep connections — with their professors, their city, and with each other.

"I used to think Uralsk was less exciting than the other cities," admits Rustam. "But now I think I was wrong. It's a different kind of exciting. It's more personal. In Almaty, you can be anonymous. Here, everyone knows you — and that's actually more motivating."

The fairest comparison might be this: Almaty is the most international, Astana is the most ambitious, and Uralsk is the most human. These are not rankings of quality but of character. Kazakhstan is rich enough in geography, history, and personality to contain all three — and to need all three.

In the end, the best city for a student is not necessarily the biggest or the most glamorous. It is the one where they grow the most, learn the most, and leave with the most to take forward. By that measure, WKU students have very little to complain about.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: If you could live in any Kazakhstani city, which would you choose?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Almaty, no question. More food, more music, more people.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I'd probably choose Almaty too — but for the mountains. They're stunning.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I'd stay in Uralsk, honestly. I've got everything I need here.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: But Almaty is more exciting than Uralsk.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: It is. But "more exciting" isn't always better. I'm more productive here.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Astana is the most modern city I've been to. But it felt colder — in every sense.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: The coldest capital in the world is not a selling point for me.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Every city has something. That's what makes Kazakhstan interesting.

vocab.definition: including people and ideas from many different countries

vocab.example: Astana's architecture is more futuristic than any other city in Kazakhstan.

vocab.definition: surrounded by land, with no access to the sea
vocab.example: Kazakhstan is the largest landlocked country in the world.

vocab.definition: not known by name; without a known author or identity
vocab.example: In a large city, you can be completely anonymous.

vocab.definition: having or showing a strong desire to succeed
vocab.example: Astana is arguably the most ambitious city in Kazakhstan.

vocab.definition: clearly different or separate from others
vocab.example: Uralsk has its own distinct character — quieter and more personal.

vocab.definition: a large flat area of land with no trees
vocab.example: Astana was built on the flat steppe of central Kazakhstan.

questions.hint: "landlocked" = surrounded by land on all sides, with no access to the sea.
